To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) academics are motivated to engage in commercialization activities for a combination of four motives, including the desire to have impact on others, and (2) these motives play different roles across fields, consistent with the different opportunity costs of commercialization and with the different payoffs of commercialization.

(1) the motives that predict patenting activities are not the same in all fields; (2) the differences in the motives that drive patenting across fields can be explained by differences in the payoff from commercial activities, and by the opportunity costs of the time spent away from traditional research.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of why scientists engage in commercial activities, and whether and how the answers to this question vary across fields.
the question of how scientists’ motives and opportunity costs affect the commercialization of their scientific discoveries.
the following questions: (a) What is the relationship between academics’ motives to engage with the commercial sector and their commercial activities?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the four motives matter, but that they matter in different ways across fields.

the results of our study are consistent with the notion of a “two-tier” system of science in the U.S.: a “core” of basic research, where the desire to have impact on others plays an important role, and an “applied” periphery, where the desire for money is the dominant force.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we find that the motives of academics to engage in commercial activity differ systematically across fields.
academics’ motives to engage with industry differ systematically across fields.
we examine how the motives to engage in academic commercialization activities differ across fields, and how these differences are related to the opportunity costs and payoffs of commercialization.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the motives for commercializing academic research differ across fields.
the four motives we study – recognition, challenge (or intrinsic motivation), money, and impact – are all related to patenting, but that their importance varies across fields.
commercial activities are not a one-size-fits-all phenomenon, and that the motives that drive academics to engage in such activities vary systematically by field of study.
